Secret program gave CIA unfiltered access to German communications

The United States Central Intelligence Agency had direct and unfiltered access to telecommunications data exchanged between German citizens, according to a new document that has surfaced in the German press.

The program, codenamed GLOTAIC, was a collaboration between the CIA and Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service, known as BND. According to German newsmagazine Der Spiegel, which revealed the existence of the program last week, it lasted from 2004 to 2006.

During those years, the CIA was given access to telephone and fax data carried by US telecommunications provider MCI Communications, which is owned by Verizon. The US-headquartered company owns a network switching facility in the German city of Hilden, located 10 miles east of Düsseldorf near the country’s border with Holland.

The existence of joint collection programs between the BND and American intelligence agencies has been established in the past, and has prompted the creation of a special investigative committee in the German parliament.

The Committee of Inquiry into Intelligence Operations was set up in 2014, after files leaked by American defector Edward Snowden revealed that the US had been spying on the telephone communications of German Chancellor Angela Merkel. But it has also been investigating whether the BND’s collaboration with American intelligence agencies violated the rights of German citizens.

The committee had previously been told that all telecommunications data given to the US by German agencies had previously been vetted by BND officers. But the GLOTAIC documents published by Der Spiegel states that audio recordings of intercepted telephone calls were “directly routed to the US” in the interests of technical efficiency.

The parliamentary committee had also been told that the data shared with the CIA concerned non-German citizens using German telecommunications networks. But the documents published last week state that a “technical glitch” in the GLOTAIC system allowed “massive German traffic” to be directly accessed by the CIA without having been first filtered by the BND.

Another document published by Spiegel reveals that the BND warned project CLOTAIC supervisors that the agency faced “serious risks” should the secret operation become public, because it had allegedly violated German federal privacy regulations.

Think Like a Tree: A New Kind of Eco-Friendly Concrete Inspired by Coral

This is something I studied a while ago because of my interest in ISRU for marine settlement and OTEC facility development. If you want to go live at sea, logically, you want to be able to build your home out of stuff you can get from the sea. There are many kinds of structures you might use. But they need to be things you can reproduce and repair aboard them and made from local materials. For a long time marine colony visionaries/proponents proposed the use of a process called electrolytic sea accretion which was developed and promoted by the eccentric Dr. Wolf Hilbertz. Basically, you would build a rebar skeleton out of magnesium--which itself can be sourced from sea water--and use it as an electrode. When low current power is applied in open water, an accretion of calcium carbonate forms on the rebar structure, slowly building up a rigid concrete-like form. The material has come to be known as Biorock

However, as the accretion builds, progressively larger currents are needed to maintain the accretion rate. In practice, no experimenters have ever been able to produce an accretion more than a few centimeters thick. But the material does attract further colonization by marine organisms and has often been explored for use in active reef restoration.

Despite its limitations, Hilbertz proposed the use of this technique for the creation of a vast marine colony called Autopia Ampere, intended for the shallow areas of the Saya de Malha Bank. This inspired a number of other marine colony visionaries such as architect Eugene Tsui with his mobile zoomorphic Nexus colony and space futurist Marshal Savage with his Aquarius colony. Eventually, though, most researchers abandoned notions of the use of this technique for construction.

Looking for more practical technology, I've long been interested in the phenomenon of 'sea whitings' where calcium carbonate spontaneously precipitates out of sea water in vast milky blooms, often in warm water locations. This is responsible for the white sand beaches in some places and is often dredged for use in making concrete. The phenomenon remains a bit unexplained but the most common idea today is that it's the product of microalgae. A variety of microorganisms accrete minerals inside them, such as calcium carbonate or silica. So, using the nutrient-rich discharge from an OTEC plant, it becomes potentially possible to culture concrete or concrete alternatives like geopolymer using industrial algaeculture techniques.

The Calera process offers a more direct chemical process where calcium carbonate (quick lime) is derived from bicarbonates and other salts and sodas from industrial byproducts combined with captured CO2 from power plants and then combined with fly ash and recycled aggregates to make an eco-concrete. This does, however, seem to be a very high-energy process and when that energy overhead is factored in its net carbon offset may not be as great as suggested. But it's very promising, if a bit too large and complex for the would-be seasteader.

Skyrim's paid mods were a debacle by anybody's standards, and it was handled very badly. But put that out of your mind for a moment.

Many years ago, there was a game called Doom. A year later, there was Doom 2 - it had a few little improvements to the engine, mostly to the lighting, but it was basically a level pack with new weapons and enemies - I look at it as the equivalent of paid DLC, but that's another discussion.

What I want to get at is that there was a huge, thriving pool of third-party developers around those two games. id contracted a few of the best to make levels for official "expansion packs". After that, there were other developers that made big, sweeping mods; some so extensive they were nearly a new game on their own, and they called those 'total conversion' mods or 'megawads'. A couple years after Doom 2, id bought the rights to two of the best megawads, and sold them as 'Final Doom'.

I see this all as very similar to paid mods, and I don't think Doom was made any worse for it - in fact, there's still an active modding community, which is pretty impressive for a game that's 22 years old. And there was, and still is, a huge amount of free mod content, of varying quality.

There were a lot of legal hassles for those third-party developers to monetize their work, though. Since they didn't own the rights to Doom, they couldn't sell expansion packs or mods directly to consumers without licensing from id, which meant getting id to take an interest to begin with, and then sorting out the legalities of either developing for id as an independent contractor, or hammering out a fair deal on selling the distribution rights to their work.

I don't necessarily see breaking down that gate as a bad thing. If third-party developers are able to sell their content on a platform like Steam, and get paid for their work while having the remuneration headaches handled for them without having to hire an accountant and a lawyer, I don't see how that's negative.

Removing the vetting process entirely meant Skyrim had the issues of people overcharging, or charging for mods that didn't work, so I think you do have to build in some kind of accountability once you remove the gatekeepers. There's lots of ways to do that don't put any additional onus on the publisher - crowd-sourced beta testing with try-before-you-buy, for instance - but with that handled, I don't see paid mods as automatically evil, and I think can actually encourage a more active and innovative modding community.

Where am I wrong?
What's your beef with paid mods?

The concept is similar to DLC, which although is in theory a good idea, has been disgustingly exploited by big games corps like EA and what not to increase profits and appease shareholders. So for some people, anything even remotely towards that concept, triggers their pent-up emotions. I'm not saying they're wrong, the concept of DLC has indeed ruined most of the game industry, but nevertheless, DLC-like concepts trigger people.

Also, with paid mods, game creators could be tempted to not try and make a fun and complete game, but just barebones features, in hope that people will create more content for it. And this is bad, because then the games market gets flooded with games that feel half-finished, with little actual content. It's great for the odd game to be designed towards modification, i.e. Gmod, KSP, etc., but there is a time and a place for it. Neither I or anyone else wants every game released to be just a boring set of barebones mechanics and foundational content, with huge gaping holes where the devs expect the public to fill in for them.

Generally, what's ruined DLC and DLC-related concepts is what tends to ruin everything - human nature.

I have no issue with third parties profiting from their own work - if they can work out a way to profit from it, more power to them.

My issue, and the reason that I fought tooth and toenail against Steam and especially Beth over the Skyrim deal - is developers and distributors controlling the market, and taking the lion's share of the profits.

First is controlling the market. I know they denied this, but still - I'm reasonably certain that, had the Skyrim deal stuck, Steam and Beth would have, sooner or later, used legal pressure to shut down any and all competing mod sources, including free ones. Their intent never was merely to profit from paid mods, but to completely control the market. Nexus likely would have remained in place, but that's because Dark0ne would've agreed to their terms, which would likely have boiled down to essentially being an official distributor. The handful of competing free mod sites would've been shut down, and free mods would eventually cease to exist entirely (other than on a pirate basis).

Second is the whole concept of the developer profiting from somebody else doing work that they explicitly chose not to do. For instance - among the most popular Skyrim mods, and one of the first to get in line for pay, is SkyUI. SkyUI exists because many people dislike the vanilla UI. And the vanilla UI exists specifically because Beth chose to put it in there. It's not an oversight or an honest mistake - they very deliberately chose to invest in exactly that UI. They explicitly decided that that was the UI that they were going to offer consumers, so that was the UI they expected consumers to pay for, and that was the UI that consumers did in fact pay for. Therefore, by my thinking, that's the ONLY UI they deserve any profit from. It's the one they chose, therefore it's the one they get to profit from and it's the one they did in fact profit from. If they wanted to profit from one as good as SkyUI, they should've included that one in the game. They didn't, and that was the choice they very deliberately made. The SkyUI team, on the other hand, DID make that UI - the UI that Beth could've made but deliberately chose not to make - so the SkyUI team are the ones, and the only ones, that deserve any profit from it. Beth deserves nothing from that UI.

And on that last - it's not simply that expecting profit from something that the devs very deliberately chose not to do is unethical, but that it will certainly only encourage even more shoddy work from the devs. It's already a problem that devs (and particularly Beth) cut corners on the PC version of their games, knowing that the community will excuse things that can be fixed by mods. Imagine how much worse it will get if they know that they not only can cut corners and count on the modders to fix things, but that they'll profit from it when they do.

So - the problem, in my estimation, isn't the mere concept of paid mods. If a modder can profit from it, that's great. The problem is developers intervening in and controlling that market, and profiting from work that they very deliberately chose not to do themselves.

Thanks for the thoughtful response, you raise an interesting point on the potential for abuse by publishers. I'd like to believe we wouldn't buy games from 'bad' publishers that release things they know are broken, but obviously we do.

I'd point out that all of this is likely moot.

It's certain that Beth and Steam have already worked out the system by which FO4 will have paid mods, from the very beginning. And I'm not going to be in the least bit surprised if it has some mechanism - whether legal or technological - that makes free mods impossible, and also from the very beginning.

I don't think the Skyrim thing was ever intended to actually remain in place. I think it was a combination of a test run and a very deliberate and calculated PR move. They had to have known that paid mods were going to be controversial and it's certain that they didn't want that shitstorm to accompany FO4's development and/or release, so they tested the idea out ahead of time, with Skyrim, in order to get the worst of the predictable anger out of the way. Then they issued a public mea culpa and withdrew the plan. That's now set the stage so that they can implement paid mods from the beginning with FO4, and do it all with a positive PR spin - they listened to the concerns of the community and blah, blah, blah... It's going to be hard to get up anything close to the amount of opposition that they got that first time again, so they'll already be ahead - they will have already limited the amount of harm it could do to FO4 by having it all directed at Skyrim months ago. And the Skyrim plan can serve as a sort of opening bid, allowing them to now come back with FO4 and offer up a plan that's just very slightly less objectionable and treat it as something that they've done "with the desires of the community in mind" or some such. For instance, one obvious move - Beth and Steam will each take a cut of the profits that's very slightly less than the one they announced with Skyrim. The original, and rightly unpopular, plan was 25% to the modder, 30% to Steam and 45% to Beth. Now they can roll FO4 out with something like 30% to the modder, 30% to Steam and 40% to Beth and pretend that they're being generous.

The thing I'll be most curious to see is if they'll implement a system to make free mods literally impossible. They could do that in the name of "curating content" or "ensuring quality" or "protecting PC security" or such - they'll "protect"us by making sure that only mods that have been properly vetted by the experts at Steam and/or Beth will be playable. I could see doing it with, for instance, some sort of key encryption. A mod in development would work, but it would only work on the particular copy of the game that was registered to the same account as that particular copy of the development kit. It would have to have some other "universal" key enabled in order to work with any other copy of the game, and that could only be done by Steam or Beth. That would eliminate the competition from free mods right off the bat, and without any need to mess about with it from a legal perspective at all.

TL/DR: It's a moot issue anyway, really. FO4, and all future Beth titles, will have paid mods, from day one.

First things first: You need to stop lumping Valve and Bethesda in the same group when you talk about this. The deal that Valve made is the same deal they've made with every single other developer: 30%. It's the same deal you get if you have something in Apple's iTunes Store and App Store. It's the same deal you get from Amazon in their app store, and Google in theirs. 30% is basically industry standard for a digital distribution platform. It's probably (although I have less experience with this) similar to physical distribution deals, as well. The remaining 70% (and how to split it with the modders) was completely in the hands of Bethesda. We'll get to them shortly. This information has been known since day one of the paid mods debacle, but a lot of people missed it.

As far as controlling the market, Valve has repeatedly proven they're not interested in a monopoly. The only thing they do that might even come close to that is requiring that games use the Steam Wallet for in-game stores, but they don't even require exclusivity. So if a game uses some kind of currency that you can buy with real money, it doesn't matter if you can also buy that currency with paypal or a credit card or whatever, so long as the in-game store uses the Steam Wallet.

Now Bethesda... they've lost all my respect and I have no interest in defending them. That being said, they did make an entire game and then released tools so that people could mess with it. That's something they didn't have to do, so they attached a license. As it turns out, the license says that modders can't actually make a profit from it unless Bethesda gives them the OK. This isn't news, by the way, and it's one of the big reasons there haven't been paid mods to date.

Bethesda is totally within its rights to restrict who gets paid piggybacking on its product. It's totally within its rights to only allow people to profit if they make a specific deal with Bethesda. It's also totally within its rights to set the terms of that deal, and to set those terms as self-serving and shitty as they want. The reason that those are its rights is because they spelled it out ahead of time in a document that every single modder had to agree to. It's kind of a dick move, sure, but it's not unethical or illegal. The flip side of this situation is that it's well within the modders' rights not to take the deal. Further, it's within the modders' rights not to develop content that will assist a (potentially shoddy) developer, if they're concerned about that.

Modding is actually prohibited most of the time in the license agreements that most people agree to without reading. The companies that allow it usually do so within specific and narrow constraints. The fact that Bethesda not only allows it but facilitates it is to their credit. The shitty deal and the way they handled it totally counts against them.

Ultimately Bethesda pulled a dick move, but it was within their rights to do and since they spelled out exactly how it was going to work ahead of time, it wasn't unethical or illegal. Part of the blowback was that they offered such a terrible, awful, shitty deal. Part of it was that a chunk of the people who took the shitty deal did so without reading it, or they read it and assumed it meant something other than what was spelled out. That's actually not Bethesda's fault. Although again, it was a shitty deal.

If a modder wants to make something that Bethesda didn't and make a profit from it without Bethesda getting a piece or having any claim to it, they have to do it in such a way that it's not covered under any of the licenses or contracts they've already agreed to. Basically, that means that they've got to develop their own game.

The bottom line is that Bethesda offered a bad, self-serving deal. That's all their good will from me. If I buy Fallout 4, it will be because at that point they've been supportive of the community, and they had a bug free launch, and they've crafted an exceptional game, and they're not doing anything shitty like trying to nickel-and-dime their customers with shitty DLC and microtransactions. I don't expect I'll be buying Fallout 4. But if you're going to hate and vilify, at least direct it at the right people and do it for the right reasons.

It is a feature that less than 10% of people would use if available under arguably the best case and there isn't any direct incentive for developers to add mod support or to make x game work nicely with steam workshop for example. That puts a significant cost on the developer to make a feature most people will not use and not care if it isn't featured. Not hard to see how addon/workshop support might be something planned initially and then dropped quickly during development.

When you have a platform that allows paid addons then there is incentive for the developers to not only add support but make sure it actually works well. Paid mods mean the original IP owner gets a piece of the pie (basically for adding support), the developer of the mod itself gets paid (I haven't seen too many people against this), and of course the distributor of the content grabs their slice as well (valve) - capitalism at its finest.

Sure, some mods which were free might cost money. In general that means you should expect better quality mods and better support. Many mods would still remain free. Think of a market similar to mobile app development - many paid and free alternatives to do similar things. I think a lot of people just saw something cost money one day that was free the day before and that really isn't a good way to bring about a new model.

Paid mods are going to be one of the only ways to really get widespread addon/mod support integrated with games out of the box. Developers have no reason to add support otherwise (and hoping for it out of the kindness of their hearts is how you end up in a situation with so few games having good mod support).

I think the issue was that instead of mods made by hobbyists for free and distributed freely, paid mods can only be distributed through authorized channels and most of payment goes to the channel, not the creator, and people using mods obtained outside that channel getting the banhammer. If paid mods were an additional option instead of the only, and if the the creators of mods, or the creator of the base game would receive a larger share instead of the distributing channel cashing in, people would probably will a lot less angry about paid mods.

Paid mods were never really a discussion until Steam tried to push it in to the spotlight. Paid mods were never really a problem. What was the problem was how steam was trying to introduce it. Steam was trying to take a cut, the game maker was trying to take a cut, and the mod maker was getting way less than half of the money.

While I can see steam taking a cut to cover distribution expenses, I don't understand why game makers seem to think they're entitled to mod profits. Especially when you're taking so much that you're basically screwing the mod creators.

I'm less opposed to it than some, but at the very least, there are two big issues they need to address before they try it again:

1) They must not do it with a game that's already been released. Selling a game with a strong implicit, or even explicit, promise of years of free mods, like Skyrim or Fallout, then changing the terms of the deal is unfair for people who bought a game with free mods then received a game with paid mods. If they're going to do it, they'd better make it clear from before people buy a game. And that's ignoring the whole issue of mod authors allowing their work to be used in other mods when it was free, then suddenly seeing those other mods using their content charging a fee.

2) Multiplayer games will have huge fragmentation issues. Imagine a game like ARMA 3, which has a lot of user-made free content and is mostly played multiplayer. A few important, popular mods going paid would split the community into a giant ven diagram of which particular mods any given server would require, and the population of all servers would suffer. Given n mods, there would be 2^n possible combinations of which mods any given server might require. With just five popular paid mods, that's 32 possible combinations of which mods might be required on any given server. I really don't see how it would be tenable in a multiplayer game unless you require all paid mods to have unpaid versions that allow non-buyers to still play in games with people who own them, and there would still be issues with pushing that content to those players.

Most mods are low quality and buggy as hell. There's no quality control over mods, thus not only can an update from the developer break a oaid mod, but one paid mod could break another paid mod. Not to mention that the developer now has less incentive to fix bugs since a modder will make a patch and they can charge for it. Basically, paid mods will 100% fuck over consumers.

Your example wasn't a mod to merge into an existing game, but rather standalone games that were modified from the original. There's nothing wrong with charging for that since all of the problems go away if it's a standalone product with its own support.

Shady possibilities like people selling someone else's work, or publishers using this to control the mod market aside, there are a couple things gamers should demand from paid mods, and I do not think they are realistically going to happen.

The first issue is compatibility. How do I know that this mod I am paying for is compatible with the other mods I use? I would absolutely expect the modder to guarantee which mods work with their paid mod, and list known issues with incompatible mods. The last thing a gamer wants is to buy something that they can't use. The problem is that this is a huge task for just one or two people, and most mods are created by individuals or small groups. Modders keeping on top of cross-mod compatibility is not likely to happen.

The other issue is ongoing support and updates. Gamers should expect to know exactly how long their mod will be supported for, and how long mod updates will take after base game updates. The last thing I want is to buy a mod that will break with a future base game update, and never have that mod updated again.

Modding moving out of the realm of "labors of love" to the space of paid products brings a world of expectations and issues that are generally beyond the capabilities of modders, and that means that paid mods are a terrible idea from the perspective of the consumer.
